title: ASIC warns scammers are using AI to spin vast webs of deception

reading.body:
This incident is an impersonation failure, but the AI systems involved were not deployed by a financial institution or media company. They were used by scammers outside any legitimate deployment context, to generate fabricated interviews, fake news articles, and deepfake likenesses of named public figures in order to promote an unlicensed investment platform. The failure is not a model producing false output by mistake, it is generative AI being deliberately applied to produce convincing false content at scale, with no legitimate operator in the chain to impose a check.

The scale reported by ASIC, tens of thousands of scam removals in a single year with percentage increases in the hundreds, shows that the barrier to producing this material has fallen low enough for scammers to industrialise it. Catching it requires either platform-level detection before content is hosted, post-publication takedown at volume, or identity verification systems that flag fabricated likenesses before they reach audiences. None of those controls prevented the specific fake Bullock-Kohler article from circulating.

What is not established is the identity of the people who created this content, what specific AI tools or models they used, or whether any platform that hosted the material knew it was synthetic.

reports.title: The fake Alan Kohler interview that shows a type of scam that’s on the rise
AI deepfake scams 'an emergency in the making' as ASIC reports rise in false investment endorsements
ASIC warns scammers are using AI to spin vast webs of deception

summary:
# Summary

A fake online article falsely depicted Reserve Bank Governor Michele Bullock having a heated confrontation with ABC finance presenter Alan Kohler over an unlicensed cryptocurrency platform called Boulder Sparhaven. This fabricated interview never occurred but represents an increasingly common scam tactic. According to ASIC research released today, AI-generated deepfakes of celebrities and politicians are being used more frequently and convincingly to promote illegitimate investment schemes. Prime Minister Anthony Albanese tops the list of impersonated public figures, followed by other politicians and financial experts including Alan Kohler himself.

Last year, ASIC removed 19,400 scams, a 182 percent increase from the previous period. Notably, phishing scams jumped 279 percent with 5,476 removals, while fake investment platforms increased 151 percent to 7,051 takedowns. Scammers typically create elaborate webs of deception using fake news articles, websites, and advertisements before luring victims into providing personal details. ASIC advises consumers to verify Australian Financial Services license numbers through its public registers before investing. Alan Kohler has called for heavy fines against platforms hosting such content and the AI models generating it.
